subtopic: GRANTS TO PROVINCES-STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO HEALTH INSURANCE AND SOCIAL SECURITY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: GRANTS TO PROVINCES-STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO HEALTH INSURANCE AND SOCIAL SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement to the house on government policy with respect to health services and health insurance.
From time to time, there have been inquiries in this house and outside as to when the government intends to proceed to implement the specific proposals placed before the dominion-provincial conference in 1945 for the development, by stages, of a nation-wide health program leading up to and ultimately including
health insurance. I am now in a position to give hon. members the desired information. I wish, however, in so doing, to place the health program in its proper perspective in relation to the government's larger and basic aim of securing for the people of Canada a national minimum of social security and human welfare.
Before the outbreak of war in 1939 considerable progress in social legislation had been made in Canada. A substantial measure of social security had been provided by the dominion through the creation of the Department of Labour and other federal labour legislation, and through the establishment of annuities, of pensions for the aged and the blind and for disabled veterans and veterans' dependents; and by the provinces through provincial departments of labour and labour legislation including workmen's compensation and through enactments related to widows' and mothers' allowances, maternity benefits, child welfare, sickness and hospitalization.
In all this, there had, however, been relatively little co-ordination of social security measures and no approach to a nation-wide plan. Even before the war it had become increasingly apparent that if there were to be an avoidance of conflict between the provinces and the Dominion on questions of jurisdiction, and unnecessary duplication of social services with consequent waste of public money, what was required was a comprehensive scheme of social insurance which, by satisfactorily combining provincial and federal services, would constitute a charter of social security for the whole of Canada.
Since the outbreak of war, there has been a tremendous advance in social security legislation. Far-reaching measures such as unemployment insurance, family allowances, floors under farm and fish prices, increase of pensions and allowances for the aged, the blind, the war veterans and their dependents, have been enacted in the federal fields, while legislation, varying greatly in degree and kind, respecting health services and hospitalization, maternity benefits, and the like has been enacted by the provinces. Notwithstanding this great advance in social services, little advance has been made towards an integration of federal and provincial activities which would combine existing social insurance measures and health services in
Health Services

a comprehensive constructive, efficient and effective nation-wide plan.
The government's policy of bringing into being a comprehensive scheme of social insurance which would co-ordinate provincial and federal activities, and which would include the establishment of a nation-wide system of health insurance was set out specifically in the speech from the throne at the opening of the session of January, 1943. A select committee of this house was thereafter appointed to examine and report upon the most practicable measures to give effect to the policy.
In the course of the general election campaign of 1945, after enumerating some of the social legislation already enacted, I stated that the government's program looked beyond these achievements to the early establishment of other great social measures. I said specifically: "The government is prepared to support a national scheme of contributory old age pensions on a basis more generous than that of the existing pensions. The government also believes that a substantial improvement in national health could be achieved through dominion-provincial co-operation. We have accordingly pledged ourselves to support a measure for federal assistance in a nation-wide system of health insurance, to include assistance to the provinces for preventive medicine. If the present government is returned to office, we shall proceed with these measures as soon as agreements with the provinces can be concluded."
Specific proposals regarding contributory old-age pensions and a nation-wide system of health insurance were made to the provinces at a conference which met in August, 1945, within two months after elections. As hon. members know, it has unfortunately thus far not proved possible to secure agreement with all the provinces.
The government has reached the conclusion that lack of agreement with certain provinces should no longer be allowed to stand in the way of a further immediate advance in the field of public health. We have accordingly decided to proceed with a substantial health program at the present session.
An important feature of the government's health program of August, 1945, was the proposal of a planning and organization grant to the provinces. This grant was designed to assist the provinces in developing their planning and organization for the improvement of existing health services, for the development of new programs that might be needed, and for the detailed planning of hospital and medical care insurance.
In addition to the planning and organization grant, the government also proposed a series
[Mr. Mackenzie King.l
of grants for the development and improvement of existing provincial health services. Grants were to be made available for the following purposes:
(a)	General public health services. .
(b)	Tuberculosis control.
(c)	Mental health care.
(d)	Venereal disease control.
(e)	Prevention and control of crippling conditions in children.
(f)	Blindness prevention and control.
(g)	Professional training.
(h)	Public health research.
In addition to these proposed health service grants, the government offered, in the 1945 proposals, to make financial assistance available 'through low-interest loans for the construction of needed hospitals throughout the country.
All these grants were regarded as essential steps in the development of adequate health services for the people of Canada, regardless of whether or not health insurance was eventually to be introduced. It was 'recognized, however, that the proposed grants would have the added advantage of being fundamental prerequisites of a nation-wide system of health insurance.
Although the introduction of these health grants was postponed, in 1946, the Department of National Health and Welfare has continued to give constant attention to the planning of health services. Studies have been carried out by the division of the health insurance studies which was established in 1945 to lay plans for the eventual introduction of health insurance. The research division of the department has also been actively engaged in this field. From time to time, specialists of outstanding ability have been asked to undertake more specific assignments. As a result of the subsequent research, certain modifications have been made, in the 1945 proposals.
I come now to the announcement of the health measures which it is proposed to take at the present session of parliament. These measures also represent first stages in the development of a comprehensive health insurance plan for all Canada. Parliament will be asked in the supplementary estimates to m-ake the necessary provision for the proposed health program.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare plans to arrange an early meeting with the appropriate technical officers of the various provincial health departments and the Dominion Council of Health to work out with
Health Services
them the detailed arrangements of the proposed health grants, and, in particular, the conditions to be attached to their adminstra-tion.
The specific proposals are as follows:
Health survey grant. The government proposes to make available immediately to all the provinces a health survey grant replacing the health and planning organization grant of $625,000 on the basis outlined to the provinces in August, 1945, as amended by the statement I made when the conference reconvened in November of the same year. The amendment was to the effect that the grants were not to be conditional upon the provinces undertaking to enter a health insurance plan.
The non-recurring grant of $625,000 is to be divided as follows: There will be a flat grant of $5,000 to each province; the balance is to be divided between the provinces on the basis of population, with the proviso that in no case shall the provincial grant amount to less than $15,000.
The purpose of this grant is to assist the provinces in setting up the machinery which will be necessary to ensure the most effective use of the other health grants now being proposed, and in planning the extension of hospital accommodation, and the proper organization of hospital and medical care insurance. Adequate safeguards will of course be provided to ensure that the provinces report in an approved manner on the expenditure of the funds and on the results of the studies undertaken.
Health grants. For the following specific purposes, annual grants will be made available to all the provinces along the lines of the proposals first outlined in August, 1945, and later amended.
1.	General public health. A grant of 35 cents per capita is proposed for the purpose of strengthening the general public health services in those areas where the provincial authorities themselves most keenly recognize the need. In succeeding years the grant will increase by 5 cents per capita, and will finally reach a peak at a rate of 50 cents per capita. These public health grants will continue from year to year, with the initial commitment amounting to approximately $4,404,000 for a full year. In order to qualify for the grants, the provinces will of course be required to maintain at least their present level of expenditures in this field. This same safeguard will be attached to all the other grants it is proposed to make.
2.	Tuberculosis control. To permit an accelerated and intensified effort directed towards the eradication of tuberculosis in Canada, the dominion government will ask parliament to make available to the provinces an annual grant beginning at $3 million and rising over a period of years to $4 million annually. The details of this grant, including the allocation of funds between the provinces, will be on the basis recommended at the time of the 1945-46 conference. The purpose of the grant will be to assist the provinces in the drive which they will now be expected to make to obtain control over tuberculosis, and to extend progressively the areas of free treatment to the maximum possible extent.
3.	Mental health care. Parliament will be asked to make provision for a similar grant to the provinces for similar purposes for mental health care amounting initially to $4 million per annum and rising over a period of years to a maximum of $7 million per annum. The seriousness of the problem of mental illness can best be illustrated by reference to the fact that between one-third and one-half of all the hospital beds in Canada today are occupied by patients suffering from mental illness.
4.	Venereal disease control. In accordance with the proposals made in August, 1945, the dominion government proposes to ask parliament to make available an amount of $500,000 annually to assist the provinces in extending and intensifying their present efforts in the control of venereal disease. Since the grants currently being made to the provinces for venereal disease control amount to $225,000 annually, the net increase under this heading will be $275,000 annually. The terms and conditions attaching to the use of this grant will be similar to those outlined in August, 1945.
5.	Crippled children's grant. Very few of the provinces have at the present time an adequately developed program for the prevention, control and treatment of crippling conditions in children. To assist the provinces in the establishment of a program in this field, and in the development of a rehabilitation and training program for crippled children, the government is proposing to ask parliament to make available the sum of $500,000 annually, to be divided on a per capita basis between the various provinces.
6.	Professional training. In order to meet the need for larger numbers of professional personnel in the public health and related health fields, the dominion government will seek appropriations to make available to the provinces an amount of $500,000 annually. It will be noted that this is twice the amount
Health Services

originally suggested in the 1945 proposals. The purpose of this grant will be to assist in making available the public health personnel which will be required in the development of an enlarged public health program in all fields. The grant will also be available to assist in developing and training the personnel required for the operation of constantly expanding hospital services.
7.	Public health research. The dominion government will ask parliament to make available to the provinces, as originally suggested in the 1945 proposals, grants for the stimulation and development of public health research. It is considered, however, that a larger amount of money than was originally proposed is justified by the expanding requirements of the field. Consequently, though the grant will be $100,000 for the first year, as originally proposed, it will thereafter be increased by $100,000 annually until $500,000 is reached. This grant is an indication of the importance the government attaches to the development of a progressive health program.
8.	Control of cancer. In addition to the grants which were originally outlined in the 1945 proposals, the dominion government is now proposing an annual grant to the provinces amounting to a maximum of $3,500,000 to assist in the development and provision of the most active possible diagnostic and treatment services for the control of the dread scourge of cancer.
First steps in the development of a plan of active control were taken a year ago in the establishment of the National Cancer Insti- ' tute, the function of which is to stimulate the development of an intensive research program in the cancer field. But research alone is not enough. More cancer clinics, more diagnostic and treatment centres are needed, if this dreadful malady is to be brought under control. The dominion government proposes to share with the provinces, on a fifty-fifty basis, the costs of any approved program for the control or treatment of cancer which the provinces may undertake. The grant will be divided on a per capita basis between the provinces.
Hon. members will note that the grants which I have thus far mentioned, with the exception of the cancer grant, correspond fairly closely with the original proposals made by the government to the provinces in August, 1945.
Hospital Construction. Before health insurance can be established on an adequate basis, another development is essential. At the present time there is a tremendous shortage of hospital beds in Canada. If, as the first stage in health insurance, hospital insurance were

now to be introduced on a contributory basis, the demand that would arise for hospital accommodation simply could not be met. This situation was recognized in August, 1945, when the dominion government offered to make available low-interest loans to assist the provinces in increasing hospital accommodation. Since 1945 the situation has not improved. The shortage still remains, amounting now to an estimated 60,000 beds of all kinds.
It is felt that the provision of low-interest loans would not at this time be a sufficient inducement to hospital construction on the scale required. Consequently, the government will seek an appropriation for outright grants towards the construction of additional hospital accommodation. These grants will amount to $1,000 per bed for active treatment beds and $1,500 per bed for chronic or convalescent beds. Analysis of the figures relating to existing shortages clearly demonstrates that the shortage of chronic or convalescent beds in Canada is most acute. As a result of this shortage, our hospitals are congested to an unreasonable degree with persons not requiring active hospital care, but perfectly capable of being treated in chronic or convalescent beds. By placing a premium on the provision for chronic or convalescent beds, which are cheaper to provide and cheaper to maintain, the congestion in active treatment units should be considerably reduced.
The proposed hospital construction grants represent, of course, only a portion of the total costs of hospital construction. The balance will have to be met by provincial grants and by local funds from other sources. One condition which it is proposed to attach to hospital construction grants is that the province shall match the dominion contribution or better it, and that the dominion contribution shall not in any case exceed one-third of the total cost per bed in any project.
The government hopes that the provinces and local communities will take the fullest possible advantage of these grants, in order that, with the least possible delay, the deficiency which now exists in hospital accommodation may be overcome. The government accordingly is prepared to recommend the appropriation throughout the next five years of the substantial sum of $13 million annually for hospital construction grants.
If the hospital construction grants are fully utilized, they will make possible provision for over 40,000 additional hospital beds in Canada. At the end of the first five-year period, the situation should be reviewed. If the hopes and expectations for the first five years are fulfilled, it is estimated that, for the sue-

Health Services
ceeding five-year period, it should be possible to reduce the annual commitment for hospital construction by approximately half.
It is estimated that the expenditure for the entire health program of which I have just given particulars, will require an appropriation by parliament over the next five years of some $30 million a year.
No doubt it will seem to hon. members that in presenting this health program to parliament the government is pursuing a policy which over the years will involve the expenditure of considerable sums of money. That is apparent. But what these expenditures may mean in the preservation of health, in the saving of human life, to say nothing of the lessening of human suffering and misery and not infrequently despair, is beyond calculation.
In commending the acceptance of this program to hon. members, I should like to remind them of the emphasis which, in the interest of the nation, all parliaments, over the years, have placed upon the conservation of the country's natural resources, and rightly so. A country depleted of its natural resources soon becomes a wilderness, a waste. But of all a nation's resources, its human resources are unquestionably the most precious. The preservation in health and strength of its population is surely the best of all guarantees of a nation's power, of its progress and of its prosperity. Our greatest national asset is the health and well-being of our people.

Mr. Speaker, we listened with some interest and with order to what the Prime Minister had to say and I ask only the same concession for myself.

This is what I had to say on April 20:
We will implement a social security program that will provide against the hazards of health and accident, as well as sickness and unemployment. We will provide old age pensions at an earlier age and on a more generous scale. We will carry out these policies, not alone by government grants as at present-we will supplement them by a contributory system to which all wall make a small payment in their earning years, thus making possible a real pension on a higher basis in the place of the present "means test" gratuity basis on which it is now paid.
Health Services

Following that address and the discussions which ensued the following statement of policy was agreed upon:
The Progressive Conservative party proposes a contributory "four-in-one" social security program available to every Canadian irrespective of occupation to provide the following benefits:
(1) Retirement pensions at age sixty-five without the means test; (2) Accident and sickness benefits; (3) Health insurance; (4) Extended unemployment insurance benefits.
Under this program citizens will by contributions made during their working years be enabled to provide protection against the hazards of sickness, accident and unemployment and be enabled to retire in decency and comfort at age sixty-five.
It is intended that this "four-in-one" social security program w'ill be established in collaboration with and be administered by the provinces.
Enabling legislation will be enacted with permissive power to the provinces to adopt the plan, thus avoiding the necessity of constitutional amendments or an immediate over-all dominion-provincial agreement.
Until the contributory plan becomes fully operative the dominion will pay at least 75 per cent of a retirement pension of $40 per month.
Family allowances on a uniform basis, regardless of the number of children in the family.
In co-operation with the provinces a national health program will be established including promotion of improved nutritional standards and effective preventive health services to assist research and control of cancer, arthritis and other diseases and to provide assistance for the construction of hospitals, health and recreational centres.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, we have had no opportunity to study the details of the program announced today by the Prime Minister, proposals that have been advanced to us without previous notice, and therefore without opportunity for debate. However, we shall study these proposals to see whether they provide a sufficiently wide social security program and to see whether the means of implementing that program are of a practical and effective character.
There are one or two questions I should like to direct to the Prime Minister, if he is in a position to answer them today. The first one is this. If this legislation is ready, why was it not announced in the speech from the throne? That is what the speech is for. It gives an opportunity for the announcement of public policy. When a policy is announced in that speech, the house is given an opportunity to discuss it. But now in the middle of the session a new program is brought forward.
The next question is this. Has the Prime Minister consulted any or all of the prov-

inces with respect to this program? If so, what indication has he had from it or them as to its acceptance?
I have one other observation to make before I sit down. In his opening remarks the Prime Minister referred to a statement of policy announced in 1945 with respect to social security, a program which he and others said at that time and since was to be dependent upon approval by all the provinces. Now he comes forward and says, "We have not the approval of all the provinces, but we are going forward without that approval."
I just wish to add this. Anything which the government is doing today, could have been done long before this time; this requirement of having the approval of all the provinces has been but an excuse for delay. The evidence of it is in the very announcement we have had today from the Prime Minister.

speechtext:
The announcement made this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), has taken the house by surprise, for the reason given by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Bracken), namely, that no announcement of this proposal was made in the speech from the throne; therefore it was unexpected. But while it is a surprise, it is none the less welcome. The view that has always been taken by the party with which I am associated' is that no matter what government is in power, if it brings down legislation which will lay the foundations of a proper social security system, in this country, we welcome it.
I regard the announcement made this afternoon by the Liberal party, through its leader, as but a beginning or foundation, of a more adequate national social security plan. My hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party tell us what they might have done under their program adopted a month ago. But I care not what government is in power; as long as' they bring down legislation that will be helpful to the people, we shall welcome it and support it.
I believe, of course, that this legislation has been popularized to a large extent because four years ago, the people of my own province elected a C.C.F. government. In that province there has been brought into existence the widest plan of health insurance that exists in this country. We welcome the Prime Minister's proposal to assist in the building of hospitals. In my own province the provision of hospital beds has presented difficulties. During the past four years the number of beds has been practically doubled, and still the accommodation is inadequate.
Health Services
One thing that struck me in connection with the research proposals suggested by the government was that the amount worked out-I made a rough calculation when the Prime Minister gave the figure-to about one cent per head of the population of the country. Many of the amounts mentioned this afternoon seemed to me to be pitifully small. We welcome the proposals, however, as the beginning of a program of health insurance and other social security measures for our people.
I want to express approval particularly of the assistance that is to be given in the fight against cancer and tuberculosis, for assistance to crippled children and for treatment of the mentally ill. Those are worthwhile proposals.
It is fortunate that we live in a democracy where from time to time there are by-elections and provincial elections. I have noticed that, for some uncanny reason, exceedingly interesting proposals are often made just about the time these events occur. Of course, I am not suggesting for a moment that any such event provided the occasion for the announcement which was made this afternoon. As a matter of fact, in preparing to take some part in these by-elections I have been reading the pronouncements of the Liberal party, beginning with 1919, on this very subject. While today's announcements may interfere with some of the speeches I thought of making, I am glad indeed that the Prime Minister, before he retires from the high office which he has indicated: he is to relinquish within a short time, has placed before the House of Commons these proposals looking to measures of health insurance and social security which were foreshadowed when he was elected leader of the Liberal party in 1919.

speechtext:
May I say at once, speaking in a general way, how pleased I am with the manner in which the program has been accepted by all parties opposite as well as by hon. members on this side. I believe that circumstance in itself will give great satisfaction to the people of Canada. After all it would be strange indeed, with the knowledge we all have of human lives and the problems of individual homes, if all of us were not deeply concerned in these questions which affect human welfare and human well-being. It is no surprise, therefore, that hon. members should have expressed, to the extent they have, approval of this program. I am indeed happy to see the unanimity of feeling there appears to be on the part of hon. members in favour of our doing what can be done by parliament, in the light of our knowledge of conditions, to bring into being in this country an effective nation-wide program of social security and health insurance.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) asked why we did not have this particular program set out in the speech from the throne. First may I say that if the hon. gentleman looks over the various speeches from the throne from 1913 up to the present he will see in each some reference to some measure of social insurance, either on the surface or to be read between the lines which

has since found its place in today's pronouncement. However I shall be perfectly frank with my hon. friend. While the speech from the throne is intended to give hon. members a lead with regard to questions which it is intended to bring before the house during the session, the speech need not necessarily include mention of all measures to be brought down. The speech itself is a formal procedure which affords to parliament the beginning of its consideration of the affairs of the session. It usually makes mention of the principal measures, but is not intended necessarily to include all the measures. As long as parliament is in session, there is opportunity for the government to bring in new measures if it so desires.
There probably would have been special mention of this program had it not been for a reason which I am sure hon. members will recall. The house was called into session much sooner than had been anticipated when we prorogued. The house met early in December because of certain emergent measures which had required very close and careful consideration on the part of the government before the session opened. In addition, as hon. members will recall, for some weeks previous, I was necessarily absent from Canada almost up to the day the house met. For these reasons it was thought desirable that we should not seek to place before the house, without very great care being given its presentation, a program which from the outset we had hoped it would be possible to set forth at this session. I think hon. members will benefit in the end from the fact that we took the necessary time to deliberate in detail upon this very large question, and present its numerous and essential features in a form which would leave no doubt as to the relation between its different parts.
My hon. friend asked about the consent of the provinces, and whether they had been consulted. We have been receiving communications from the provinces right along asking when we were going to bring in these specific proposals. I would not like to say how many communications have been received, or to attempt to give their details; all I can say, speaking generally, is that most of the provinces have I believe been asking when the proposals would be brought in. The reply given was that we hoped to bring them in as soon as we could get the provinces generally to agree.
If we have delayed in this matter, it is because we had hoped and expected that all the provinces would eventually join with us. I cannot yet understand why the two largest provinces in this country have not found it possible, as have the other seven, to join with

Health Services
this government in working out plans such as have been presented today. If there has been some delay, as I say, it has been because we were waiting in the hope and expectation that when this program was presented to parliament it would be possible to say, in connection with it, that all the provinces had been in conference.
That has not been possible. We have, however, waited as long as we thought we should. However, in what we are now presenting it will, I believe, be seen that if there has been a delay, no province is likely to suffer very much as a result.
I suggest to my hon. friend that I do not think he will find the word "all" in any statement made as to the consent or agreement of the provinces. The words "the provinces" have been used, but the word "all" was carefully avoided in any statement that was made. That was only the part of political wisdom. It might have happened that it was not the two largest provinces that had failed us, but that one of the smaller provinces had slipped up, and that as a consequence matters for all the others would have been held back. I give my hon. friend a word of counsel. It is always wise to try to anticipate all possibilities before they arise. In so doing you do not find yourself unnecessarily embarrassed when the important moment comes.

LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): With respect to the first of the hon. member's questions, I am sure that all hon. members and all citizens of free democracies in the world realize that the world is indebted to the government of the LTnited Kingdom for the burden it has carried for so many years in the administration of the Holy Land. Inquiries oj the Ministry
being disorder in the Holy Land upon the retirement of the British forces. subtopic: WINDING-UP OF BANK AND REPEAL OF THE PENNY BANK ACT

speechtext:
Mr. R. W. MAYHEW (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 221, to provide for the winding-up of the Penny Bank of Ontario and the repeal of the Penny Bank Act.
He said: I desire to give a short explanation of this bill. The bill is to provide for the winding-up of the Penny Bank of Ontario, and repeal of the Penny Bank Act, 1927. The Penny Bank of Ontario was incorporated by letters patent dated April 19, 1904. In 1942 the bank stopped accepting deposits, to avoid competing with the government sale of war
Penny Bank Act
savings stamps and certificates to school children, and no deposits have been accepted since that- time. May I say that the request for the winding-up of this bank did not come from the government; it came from the directors of the Penny Bank of Ontario itself. When the act is repealed it will be necessary to take certain steps, and I shall try to enumerate them. But first I should like to say a word on behalf of the department. They have appreciated the work of this bank. It has done a great service to the province of Ontario. It is true that only one province, namely, Ontario, has availed itself of the provisions of the act. It is thought wise to repeal the act once the Ontario bank have repealed theirs.
The steps that will have to be taken after this bill is passed will be as follows: one, the winding-up of the bank will be under the supervision of the inspector general of banks; two, the assets will be realized; three, the bank will discharge its liabilities; four, the bank will advertise, in the areas in which it carried on business, that it is being wound-up; five, on August 1, 1948, or on a later date if the Minister of Finance so decides, the bank will transfer to the post office savings bank an amount necessary to meet the aggregate of deposits of SI or more; six, repay to the members of the bank amounts that they had paid into the guarantee fund and release other members from any liability to the bank pursuant to a subscription to the guarantee fund; seven, deposits of less than SI which have remained dormant for five years will be extinguished; if not having remained dormant they will be transferred to the post office savings bank; eight, any amounts remaining after providing for the foregoing will be transferred to the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto. The amount that will be transferred to the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto will likely approximate $84,000 or $85,000. This will be the residues of moneys that have been earned and those that have lain dormant in the bank, which it would be pretty nearly impossible to distribute on any equitable basis.

subtopic: WINDING-UP OF BANK AND REPEAL OF THE PENNY BANK ACT
speechtext:
We are now on second reading of Bill No. 221, to provide for the winding up of the Penny Bank of Ontario and the repeal of the Penny Bank Act. I wish to point out one or two matters in connection with it, because no doubt the minister has had some requests for the winding up of this bank.
I am sorry to see this old penny bank wound up. It has had a long history in our city. It was the old public school board in
Toronto that started this splendid work years ago. One of the founders was the late C. A. Brown, formerly chairman of the public school board. One of the advantages of it was that it encouraged savings and thrift among the school children who were in our city schools. If I may be permitted to say so, one of the glories of the Victorian era was that the people kept the state. Now, apparently, the principle is being changed; the state keeps the people. There never was a time in history when the lessons of thrift and savings were more important than they are at the present time. "Save the pennies and the dollars will look after themselves", used to be one of the favourite mottoes on the walls of the loan and saving companies. Workers used to go to the offices of these companies every Saturday night to deposit their 50 cents, $1 or $1.50, or some small fraction of their earnings.
It would be well for the government to reconsider its policy with regard to the penny bank and have it re-established on a new and better basis as part of the educational system of the country.
I am glad to see that section 4 provides that the residue is to go to a great and glorious cause, the Toronto Hospital for Sick Children, founded by the late John Ross Robertson, a great Canadian patriot who spent the best years of his life on public health and the Hospital for Sick Children, which has been such a blessing to our city and to our country. John Ross Robertson was one who in a long well-spent life of service and sacrifice served his God, his king and his country most faithfully and well.
I hope the government will consider this constructive suggestion and thus provide for future generations an important lesson on thrift and saving, which should be more necessary in the world to come than it has been in the past.
This matter was discussed this week at a large meeting of representatives from the school boards from all over Canada, held in the Chateau Laurier. I suggest that the principle I have espoused, of re-establishing the bank for the future on a new basis, should be taken into consideration. To recognize it and act upon it would be a blessing to the country.
The house of Commons in these days does not think in terms of pennies; it is dealing all the time in millions and billions, and when people soar away up in the sky like that, it is hard for them to come down again. There is an old Scottish saying, which the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) will remember: When you go up in the clouds be sure you keep one foot on the ground; but
Penny Bank Act

that does not seem possible when people are dealing with the astronomical figures that this house deals with now. No wonder the penny bank is being abolished. The government does not encourage thrift nowadays. It takes not only pennies but bigger sums and uses them to send people around the seven seas on useless trips of all kinds, duplicating and not reducing expenditures.
I hope that in the recess the government will consider a bill such as I have suggested, and that the Minister of Finance will introduce at the next session a measure national in scope, which will furnish a means whereby the children can save and be encouraged in the thrift which seems to be lacking everywhere today.

subtopic: WINDING-UP OF BANK AND REPEAL OF THE PENNY BANK ACT
speechtext: I wish to make just one or two comments on the bill. With much of what the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has said I can agree, though I cannot follow his conclusion, because I do not think that any other course than that which is proposed could be adopted. Like him, 1 feel that the winding up of this useful institution is perhaps an indication that thrift is not as highly regarded nowadays as it used to be. Indeed, the very fact that in common parlance we call a halfpenny a penny, when what we have in mind is a cent, is an indication that unconsciously the value of money has shrunk. I join with the hon. member in regretting the necessity for the step that is being taken; nevertheless, when you look at the situation as it is and consider that the public-spirited people who have been carrying on this enterprise have decided that it must be wound up, there is no other course, it seems to me, for the government to take. ' This, it has been explained to me, is virtually a private bill which for constitutional reasons has come in as a government measure. As to the details of it, now that I am on my feet I might make one or two comments. As I understand it, it is proposed to return to the depositors what they have deposited, with the exception that special provision is made with regard to deposits of less than one dollar made by persons who have not been heard from for years, and the balance over and above the amount contributed by these public spirited founders is to be given to the sick children's hospital in Toronto, which, as has been pointed out, though it is referred to as a Toronto institution, does in fact serve the whole province of Ontario. Therefore the claims of the depositors have been fully taken care of, and whatever balance there is is being handed over to an institution which I think carries the approval of everybody.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Notice to be published.

subtopic: WINDING-UP OF BANK AND REPEAL OF THE PENNY BANK ACT

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved the second reading of Bill No. 248, to provide for carrying into effect the treaties of peace between Canada and Italy, Roumania, Hungary and Finland.

subtopic: MEASURE WITH RESPECT TO TREATIES BETWEEN CANADA AND ITALY, ROUMANIA, HUNOARY AND FINLAND
speechtext:
I just wish to take two or three minutes of the committee's time in connection with Bill No. 248 to provide for carrying into effect the treaties of peace between Canada and Italy, Roumania, Hungary and Finland. As I mentioned the other day, the people of Finland have always loved liberty and freedom. They were and are a fine people and a great many of them came to Canada before the second war. I pointed out also the other day that Russia secured a port in Finland and one in Norway, the port in Finland being at Petsamo. Hungary and Roumania have become Soviet satellite states and many of their people have been deported as slaves by the Soviets. There are several textbooks in the library dealing with the importations of these people by Soviet powers to work in the mines and breakwaters and many other things in the Arctic circle, for what reason I do not known I noticed in the press in the last few days a discussion as to whether a military power could carry out warlike operations if war came-and we hope that it will never come again-in that north Canadian Arctic circle. Surely the government must have some information about the number of these slaves who have been imported out of Hungary, Roumania and these satellite states to the country I named, awray up there in the north country and for what purpose; why they are working as slaves along the lines I indicated. The same thing applied to Italy as well until after their election there.
As I pointed out the other day, we have acquired the power of signing treaties separately. I never believed that it would be a good proposition for a country like Britain which, with her dominions, is vastly superior in natural resources, raw materials and manufacturers and many other ways, to either the United States or Russia. I never could understand why we did not hang together and declare a policy, as we did in two wars, regarding these particular countries and regarding these peace treaties. As Clemenceau, a former president of France, and some others have said, it is hard to make a treaty wdth Britain because she speaks with so many voices the world over. For that reason I think the government should tell us what their policy is. We have seen the policy of the government- we have no commitments; parliament will decide-regarding these treaties. That is what was said in San Francisco, or as declared there, where we gave one great power nation the power of veto. We know that the division of Europe wras agreed upon at Potsdam and
Treaties oj Peace

Yalta and many other places where the leaders of the three countries, the United States, Britain and Russia, met to divide up the territory of Europe after the war and declared w-hat was the power of the nations who had been in the war. We became just a minor state regarding these treaties. What had we to say about them? Little or nothing. We were told down at the united nations in New York, when the announcement was made, that we had very little to say in the peace terms. In connection with this Bill No. 248, I want to say that if the dominions had stood by the mother country, we would have had something to say in the peace treaties and we would not have let the mother country become a second-class power, two little islands on the edge of Europe.
I opposed the doctrine which was laid down shortly after the first war, shortly after I entered this House of Commons in 1922 and 1923, when it was proposed to divide Britain's representation along the lines that some of my friends in my own party supported at the close of the last war, proclaiming that in the treaty of Versailles and many other matters like that Canada should sign its name separately to treaties when we have no military force to enforce the first line of the treaty,
I can only say that I see very little effect in what we shall have. We shall have only the minor part of a small nation. In San Francisco they divided the rich and the poor, the halt, the lame, and the blind, between the nations. They decided there that they would give to one great nation the veto power, and at the present time Russia is carrying it out in a disastrous way for the peace of the world. She has made a new peace pact proposal this week. Well, beware; because once bitten, twice shy; it would be a mistake to take seriously such appeasement proposals. If we close up for a year that institution at Lake Success, we might have some peace for years to come.
Regarding our signature to these treaties, I fail to see how it will result in help for the sick and suffering in Roumania and Hungary, countries which have become slave satellite states of Russia. According to some of the textbooks to which I was referring in the library, the number runs into a million or more. We should have some declaration by the government. Have they any information as to how many of these people in Roumania and Hungary, and to a minor extent in Finland, are being taken and placed in these slave camps up in the northern part of the Soviet country?
I do not think anything said here or any other place would do very much toward giving us any say in the making of these treaties. Any 
part we have will be very minor. We shall be told about it afterwards, as we were told about the agreements reached at Yalta, Potsdam, Moscow and so on.
That shows the folly of trying to make peace or obtain security by such methods at Lake Success. What security have we achieved at Lake Success? Have we been able to end the civil war in India, or Palestine, or get on better with Russia? Have we improved the condition in many other countries which are almost in a state of war? We may sign these treaties, but they cannot be enforced because we have no force to do .so. All we can do is look pretty and pretend, as they are pretending at Lake Success, that we have security when there is no security at all. As Mr. Churchill has said, as Mr. Attlee has said, as Mr. Truman has said, and as General Bradley, the United States chief of staff, told a committee in Washington the other day, we are just as close to war as we were a few years ago, notwithstanding all the pretending we have done at Lake Success and other places.

subtopic: MEASURE WITH RESPECT TO TREATIES BETWEEN CANADA AND ITALY, ROUMANIA, HUNOARY AND FINLAND
speechtext:
As I read this resolution, its purpose is to enable the governor in council to take such steps as may be necessary to put into effect the terms of the peace treaties to which parliament agreed last session. When the treaties were before the house at that time my recollection is that our position in Canada with respect to them was somewhat uncertain, though I am speaking from memory at the moment since I have not a single note before me. I believe the minister rather clarified the situation at that time and indicated that it was the opinion of this government, and some other governments closely allied with us in matters of this kind, that we should proceed to give approval to the treaties which had been agreed to at Paris.
At that time some question was raised as to whether or not we should consider and approve the treaties, but after hearing the explanation of the minister I was convinced that our proper course was to agree to them, and we did so. At that time, if my memory still serves me aright, there was some disposition on the part of the government to withhold deposit of the ratification of these treaties until the picture had become somewhat clearer, particularly with respect to central and other European countries.
At this stage I should like to ask the minister, when he rises to reply, to tell us when these ratifications were deposited; and if he happens to have with him the dates that will be so much better. Many of us who were simply laymen in these matters were concerned because of the changed conditions which were so obvious in at least some of the

Treaties of Peace
states with which we were concluding treaties. In Hungary, particularly, as hon. members know, a communist-controlled government with, as I believe some observers have pointed out, the support of not more than seventeen per cent of the people, had achieved office. Naturally, for that reason the people of this country felt we should go slowly in any further moves respecting the approval of the peace treaty, in case that change of government should bring about some change in our relations to the country as a whole. Following the Paris conference, of course, Roumania found herself in a peculiar position and became dominated by communist influence. We all remember that not so long ago the king of that country found it necessary or advisable, whatever may be the proper term, to abdicate, so that today he is no longer the reigning sovereign.
Then, of course, we come to the question of Finland, a country which has had a pretty checkered career since 1939. That checkered career has not always been of her own making, but Finland today certainly is not the envy of any nation of the world, in view of the obvious pressure which has been brought to bear by her powerful neighbour, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. I think Finland must be congratulated on standing out as long as humanly possible against the great pressure that has been exercised against her; but she is a small nation right beside one of the major powers of the world. For that reason, of course, we may expect almost anything to happen, having in mind what has happened to other states coming within the Russian orbit.
Other changes have taken place since the Paris conference. Had we been in session some months ago, we would have been expressing fears and suspicions with respect to the Italian situation. Fortunately for democracy, in its free elections only a few weeks ago that country left no doubt in the minds of the people everywhere that if the people are aroused, if elections are free, and if democracy is allowed to function as it should, the people prefer democracy to communism, in spite of all the pressure that no doubt was applied to that country in common with the other nations of Europe.
Prior to the Italian elections, the United Kingdom and the United States made certain suggestions and proposals which I think at the time were favourably received by the Italian people. One of those proposals was that the free territory of Trieste-this was part of the settlement of peace between the allied powers and Italy at the Paris conference-should be restored to the Italian people. No doubt that was one of the diplomatic moves which was
acceptable to the Italians at that time, and no doubt it still is. Some suggestion has been made with respect to making the peace a little easier so far as the African colonies go, but I am not as familiar with that. When the minister replies in this debate I should like him to indicate what the position is now with respect to the two powers' proposal for the restoration of the free territory of Trieste to the Italian people. As a matter of fact, I think when a question was asked the minister of external affairs in the house about that time his answer seemed to indicate that, while the Canadian government might not be primarily implicated in such a proposal, nevertheless it seemed to go along with the other two great powers.
That brings me to another point. By the effluxion of time a great change has taken place in the governmental complexion of nearly all the four nations, with the possible exception of Italy. I am wondering whether, in view of that fact, changes have been suggested. Nations like Hungary, nations like Roumania and nations like Poland can no longer be termed separate, independent sovereign powers as we once understood independent and sovereign powers to mean. Surely that is one of the things we have to take account of in our dealings with what might be called the satel-litic countries of Russia.
Communism when it puts its arms around a nation never lets that nation go so long as those arms remain strong. The result is that we have now not free and independent nations bordering on the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics; we have the amalgamation of government after government under the flag of communism and under no other flag. In those countries are still people with democratic ideals and democratic objectives. Perhaps we in this country should not be too hard upon those nations particularly upon those sections of people who perhaps in the years that lie ahead may be the nucleus for the revival of democracy in central and eastern Europe.

subtopic: MEASURE WITH RESPECT TO TREATIES BETWEEN CANADA AND ITALY, ROUMANIA, HUNOARY AND FINLAND
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Danforth so very aptly properly and characteristically says they are smothered. Nevertheless we have to treat governments as we find them. I am w'ondering whether we can continue to treat these governments in the same way as we treat other governments all over the world. They are not synonymous in their position with other free and independent governments. In other words we must in the future recognize that these people are under the red flag of communism and for that reason
Treaties of Peace

they must be treated at least until they can revive their democratic systems in that particular way in that particular manner and in that particular fashion.
I want to say something now because I raised this point in a previous debate. I do not want to be regarded as one who is attempting in any way to raise questions about what are officially friendly powers. However I get pretty tired and I think the public is getting pretty tired too with the kind of propaganda that is being carried on in this and other countries. This propaganda which could be called war-mongering is carried on by communist agents and those responsible for the communist line. I am disgusted at times to find our democratic freedom allowing that kind of thing to go on in the way it has.
On the other hand we must not in this country allow ourselves to adopt an attitude or a policy which will be so akin to theirs that we may be regarded as being no better than they are. But there comes a limit to how far a country can allow those who are diplomatically immune to carry on anything more than the normal diplomatic relations between countries. The diplomatic service of the world was built up before there was such a thing as nations which not only had their own territorial ambitions but for some reason or another were not satisfied but wanted to use all means at their disposal that might be legal to see if they could not upset the governments in those countries where they had diplomatic representation.
There comes a limit to how far we can possibly allow that kind of thing to go on. I have no doubt but that the government and the ministry are alert and alive to the situation but I want to tell the committee and the government that certainly when the Dominion of Canada sends a representative to another country he should leave the system of government that exists there severely alone. The kind of government that another country either deserves or wants or merits is none of our business. But we ask other countries to do the same thing to us. What is sauce for the goose is surely sauce for the gander in international affairs the same as in agricultural matters.
I should like to see an end to all this international trouble-making. I do not want to be suspicious of any nation but I have studied the report of the espionage committee and I have watched various things that have happened. People have come to me and said that there was a certain liaison between some of the states in central and eastern Europe

and their communistic supporters here and that from time to time they had intimidated perhaps not directly but certainly indirectly certain democratic people in Canada who had relatives over there.
I think the time has come for a showdown with respect to at least some of these diplomatic immunities and some of these diplomatic representatives. We do not ask them to do anything more or less in Canada than we ourselves are prepared to do in other countries. Our embassies must never be allowed to act in such a way as to be accused even indirectly of having the slightest thing to do with anything that looks like espionage. Not only is that important in our diplomatic relations, but it is our people's job to leave other governments alone. Most nations have enough to do looking after their own governments, and, Mr. Chairman, we have that problem here ourselves at times. If we can make a good job of our own government and our own democratic system in the Dominion of Canada, that will be about enough, for the present in any event, for our people to look after.
I think it can truly be said to the great credit of our diplomatic corps generally that I have never heard even a breath of suspicion, and I hope I never shall, with respect to the kind of representation they give in other countries. But so far as other countries are concerned, particularly those which are pressing for a different political and economic system in other countries in which they have embassies and representation, I suggest, and I am very serious in my suggestion, that somehow or another we must see to it that those embassies and their representatives are giving the same kind of representation that we are giving in other countries. I think it is no more than just and proper for us to ask that.
These are just impromptu observations; nevertheless I feel keenly about the matter. I think we as a nation have probably as friendly an outlook and as peaceful ambitions as any other nation in the world. Our people in their daily life and by nature are a peace-loving people, and it annoys me and must agitate people generally across Canada to think there may be other people in the world who do not think likewise. I certainly believe that this nation has a great function to perform in securing and preserving world peace. As has been so forcefully pointed out by many much better qualified and more eloquent than I, there are no aims, national or international, which this country has which cannot be gratified by peace.
I want to ask the minister one other question, if I may, with respect to clause 3 of the

Treaties oj Peace
bill. The powers which he is now seeking from parliament by this clause are very broad. The clause reads:
The governor in council may make such appointments, establish such offices, make such orders or regulations and do such things as appear to him to be necessary for carrying out the treaties, and for giving effect to any of the provisions thereof.
I think it would be of interest to the committee to have the minister explain just what parts or provisions of the peace treaties will require this authority to be exercised by the governor in council. Perhaps the minister would also inform the committee why this particular fine and term of imprisonment have been decided upon. I have no great objection to the clause, but when we had the united nations bill before us containing a similar clause, if my memory serves me aright, major amendments were offered with respect to fines, imprisonment and the like. I am not so sure but that the provision contained in section 5 of the bill with respect to laying before parliament every order or regulation was not also amended.
I did not intend to say much about this bill and I have gone perhaps a little further than the minister expected me to do, but I do not apologize for taking up the time of the house because, when I believe a thing, I am apt to tell the world about it, and that is what I have done on this occasion.

speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister one or two questions on this clause. I think it is a matter of some importance. The small number of members present, who may be regarded as the elite of parliament, will at any rate give attention to this point. Clause 3 states:
The governor in council may make such appointments, establish such offices ... as appear to him to be necessary.
There are two questions I wish to ask the minister, and the hon. member for Peel has anticipated one of them. What kind of things is it that we shall likely have to be doing to contribute to the carrying out of these treaties?
My second question is this, and as the minister was formerly minister of justice he will be able to enlighten me. If you read clauses 3 and 4 together you will see that the governor in council is able virtually to create criminal offences without parliament having any idea up to the present of what kind of things will be made criminal offences. I do not want to be an alarmist about this, but I ask the minister whether this is the usual method of legislating, and whether he, in his capacity as a member of the legal profession and as a former minister of justice, approves this indirect way of creating offences in respect of people who afterwards may be heavily punished.
Clause 5 provides that these regulations shall be laid before parliament, but I do not understand from that that parliament has any power at that time to alter them in any way. However, that does not seem to me to be so relevant. The chief point of my question is to ask the minister whether I am correct, first of all, in sajdng that this gives to the cabinet, the governor in council, the power to make criminal offences by executive act, and whether that seems to be the sound way of doing it.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Perhaps I might deal with the observations that have been made by hon. members who have spoken. First of all, there are those made by the hon. member for Broadview. Although I do not agree with him, I can sympathize with his point of view. I remember a few years ago visiting the Peribonca district depicted by Louis Hemon in "Maria Chapdelaine", but it had changed. Some would regret the change that had taken place, but it was none the less real. The hon. member for Broadview must admit that things have changed since the time there was only one signature affixed for the British empire to
Treaties oj Peace

international treaties. Some may regard that as an undesirable change. I am not going to argue the matter with the hon. member for Broadview at this time. The change has occurred, and I do not think we are apt to retrace the steps that have brought about the change.
The hon. member for Peel asked what were the dates of the deposits of the ratifications. That of the treaty with- Italy was deposited on September 15, 1947, and the other three on September 19, 1947. The hon. member is right, that when the treaties were approved there was a declaration made that the time for depositing the ratifications had not yet been determined, and would be determined in consultation with the other powers which had signed the same treaty. The matter that was then foremost in our minds was the date for the deposit of the ratification of the treaty with Italy. The government of Italy was hesitating about accepting the provisions of the treaty, and it was only after some harmony had been brought into the councils of the then government of Italy in respect to that, that the other signatories to the treaty arranged for a date when they would, practically all of them, at the same time deposit their ratifications. The same was done with respect to the other three treaties.
It is unfortunate, I think, for the democratic peoples of the world that in Roumania and Hungary there have occurred these seizings of power by governments which we regard as totalitarian communist governments relying upon the power of the police to keep themselves in office. Fortunately the same thing has not occurred in Italy. I think the democratic peoples of the world were quite elated to find that in Italy, there having been a free election conducted in an orderly way, the Italian people chose to remain with the western democracies. I believe we were delighted at their desire to remain with us, and we hope that from now onward their paths will parallel ours in the maintenance of free democratic institutions.
The hon. member for Peel asked what has happened with respect to the proposal of the United Kingdom, the United States and France that the peace treaty with Italy be revised to return to Italy what had been set aside as the free territory of Trieste. That has not made very much progress. Approaches have been made to the Soviet government to fix a date for a meeting to discuss a protocol to modify the treaty. I am hopeful that such a meeting will be arranged. It is well known that most of the signatories to the treaty are now of opinion that the system

which had been devised for Trieste has not been respected. They envisaged a really free territory of Trieste without interference from the two neighbours. They found that that was not going to operate, and that there would not be the kind of free territory that the treaty envisaged. I think that is the reason they came to the conclusion-and we also came to that conclusion-that the only practicable solution would be to replact that territory under the administration of the Italian government.
The hon. member asked about the former colonies. That matter is still being carefully investigated by the council of the foreign ministers, and we must confess that things are being dealt with, not in the manner we would like best, but in the manner which the circumstances seem to make it necessary for us to acquiesce in as being the ones best calculated to obtain results. I do not know what will become of the former Italian colonies. I think it is a fact that there is an over-population of the Italian mainland and of Sicily, and that there is there a high birth rate that is bringing about a situation where annually large numbers of men find that they should go somewhere else. There is not really enough living space there for them to exercise fully their activities. When they had colonies that surplus of population emigrated to the colonies. Prior to that, many of them emigrated to the western hemisphere, both North and South America. There is, I think, a larger force of manpower in Italy than can be profitably used to the full extent of its capabilities.

speechtext:
Yes, I was.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: At that time it was explained that, the treaty of course having been approved by the houses of parliament and ratifications of His Majesty having been deposited, the governments were bound, but under our system the nationals in Canada
Treaties of Peace
do not become obligated to the terms of the treaty by virtue of its ratification. In ithe United States when a treaty is ratified it becomes part of the law of the land and imposes obligations on United States citizens. Under our system, though the governments may bind themselves, it requires legislation to impose obligations upon our nationals. Some of that legislation is within our competence in the dominion parliament; some of it may be within the competence of provincial legislatures, as was decided by the privy council in the reference of 1936.
There are provisions in these treaties to attempt to restore the rights of Italian nationals in patents, for example, that were operative in Canada. There are provisions to restore the rights of Canadian nationals in patents that they might have had that were operative in Italy. There are provisions dealing with ithe settlement of debts, providing that the period of the war shall be excluded from the normal period of statutory limitation. There are also provisions that the assets of Italians vested in the custodian of enemy property may be held and appropriated by the custodian to satisfy the claims of Canadian individuals, and provisions for the collecting of these claims and adjudicating upon their substance to determine what distribution can be made in satisfaction of such claims.
It is for matters of that kind that this legislation is required. As to the form, the legislation is practically copied from the statutes that were passed in 1919, 1920 and 1922, those of 1919 and 1920 having been recommended to parliament by the Conservative government of that time, and that of 1922 having been recommended to parliament by the then Liberal government, in exactly the same form.
The hon. member asked what officials it may be necessary to appoint. Mr. Chairman, I have just one observation to make about the bill. It concerns the spirit that exists in the legion, concerning its members. Many men who have abided by the law and the regulations and have obeyed the orders given to them by their commanding officers are thrown aside by the

But there are some men who have not signed for overseas service but have gone overseas according to the orders they received. I remember such cases, and one in particular, of a man who had not signed for overseas service but was sent overseas and did his duty, and when he came back he was not even given the preference granted to military men by the civil service commission. The general legislation which permits the issuance of such kinds of charters is not, in the opinion of the Secretary of State's department, appropriate for this kind of an organization. For some time there has been a fear existing that there would be a responsibility, a legal responsibility and liability, upon the central body by reason of some act of a branch. Perhaps there was some fear of some responsibility upon the branch by reason of actions of somebody at the centre. At any rate, after long consideration the members of the Canadian Legion concluded, as many organizations do from time to time, that it was desirable they should operate hereafter under a dominion charter.

I always dislike to see the control of any organization slipping from the hands of the rank and file membership to the executive body. I do not think it is good business, and that is what I see in this particular case. I may be wrong. I think their separate councils can legislate for themselves through their conventions and through their constitutions. They have ample safeguards there.
