speechtext: Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I was explaining the resolution, which is very simple. Its purpose is to extend for one year more the measure we passed last year to pay supplementaries to the rural mail contractors. There is only one line to the bill, extending the date to March 31, 1949.

subtopic: MAIL CONTRACTS-SUPPLEMENTAL PAYMENTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last year, on February 12, the hon. Postmaster General moved a similar resolution, reading:
That it is expedient to present a bill to authorize the payment of moneys under a mail contract, supplemental to the amount agreed to be paid under the contract, and for the continuance of the payment of bonuses in respect of mail contracts, presently authorized by order in council, as supplemental payments under the proposed act.
On that resolution there was considerable discussion in the house with reference to mail contracts and the obligations of mail couriers, in which a great number of members, representing almost every constituency in Canada, took part. There was a general request at that time that a special committee be set up to look into the problems of the rural mail couriers throughout Canada. Not only one but several members urged upon the Postmaster General the setting up of a special committee for that purpose, and the Postmaster General said, at page 360 of Hansard:
I have no objection to having a committee consider this matter in an effort to improve the service.
You will note, Mr. Chairman, that at that time the Postmaster General was rather in favour of a special committee being set up. One year passed, and then on February 10, 1948, I directed this question to the Postmaster General and the Prime Minister. It will be found at page 1039 of Hansard of February 10, 1948:
Is it the intention of the government to set up a special committee of the house to study
the problems of the rural mail couriers in order to give these most faithful servants a living wage ?
The Postmaster General replied:
It is not the intention of the government to establish a committee, but as I said before, a bill will be brought in to give authority to make further supplementary payments.
I am at a loss to understand the reluctance of the Postmaster General to having a special committee set up in the best interests of his own department. It is difficult to understand why such a committee should not have been set up to study this serious problem this session. Otherwise how are the rural mail couriers to know where they stand with reference to their contracts? They have no security whatsoever once their contract expires. Very few officials of the government stand in that position and I think it is time that we gave consideration to these faithful mail couriers. If we give them no support at this time, once their contract is expired, we can say of them, "The last state of that man is worse than the first." That is the position we are leaving our mail contractors in today.
The mail couriers are not looking for large remuneration. All they are looking for under present-day conditions is a living wage. But they would like to have a little security after their long years of service, so that under the present obnoxious tender system they would not find themselves, at the end of their contract, dispensed with for the sake of a $5 bill on a four-year contract. That is the position they are in today. I suggest to the Postmaster General that we get rid of this obnoxious tender system and that a new and better system be set up which will give the mail couriers a certain amount of security as well as a living wage.
Suppose, for instance, we start with a mileage basis of $50 per mile for the carrying and distributing of mail on an improved highway. If it is an ordinary dirt road the mail courier should be allowed something extra per mile for travelling at a disadvantage over an unimproved road. In addition to this basis of $50 per mile, there should also be taken into account the number of boxes served and the number of post offices. Consideration should also be given to the time required for .the delivery of the mail. If consideration were given to these three factors I am sure that our mail couriers would be 100 per cent satisfied, and the cost to the country would be very small. Let us not forget that these men are the most faithful servants of any department in the government of our country. Why should we ask them to put in twenty-five years' service, and a few of them have longer service than that, or it may be twenty years' service,
Postal Service

or fifteen, and then at the end of their contract period because someone tenders to do the work for five dollars, or it may be one dollar less, they are out. They have no security under the present tender system, and they are .poorly paid.
The cost of their equipment should also be taken into account. True, on a good highway they can use an automobile during the summer months, but that is an expensive article today. Even if they buy second-hand ones, the repairs and so forth are expensive. We as a committee should urge upon the department the necessity of taking into consideration the extra cost to which these couriers are put at this time, and they should be reimbursed for it.
We might look at another side of the question. In my own constituency there are several couriers-one in particular-with a thirty or thirty-one mile route. Last winter was a very hard one, and there was no opportunity whatsoever to use a car, even if they had one. Under those conditions the courier I have in mind was forced to use two horses to continue his work. He did his work faithfully and well. Have hon. members ever considered what it takes to feed two horses at the present time? It costs 100 per cent more than it did a few years ago. When this man was finished at the end of the month and took his expenses into consideration I doubt whether he would have fifty cents left for himself. Hon. members may say that that was because of a very hard winter in the east, but that is apt to occur at any time. We should do something for these men, and do it now.
If the resolution which is before us goes into effect tonight, what will it do? It will assure the mail courier that he will have his little bonus extended to him as before, but it gives him no security whatsoever at the end of his contract. I have already said, and I repeat that he loses his position after probably fifteen or twenty years' service because of a somewhat smaller tender, or a tender $5 or $10 less than his.
For a moment I should like to refer to the great discrepancies that exist between the mail contracts in the constituency of Queen's. I hold in my hand a list of rural mail contracts in my constituency, and I want to bring it to the attention of the Postmaster General. These mail routes are of the same length, and possibly the same number of boxes are served; yet there is this great difference. On an eight-mile route the average price paid is from $300 to $400. On a nine-mile route the average price paid is from $400 to $450. On a ten-mile route the average is from $372 to $400. On a fourteen-mile route the average

is from $564 to $700. On a sixteen-mile route the average is from $638.97 to $1,000. On a nineteen-mile route the average is from $668.31 to $925. On a twenty-six mile route the average is from $902.50 to $1,450. They are all different. On a twenty-eight mile route the average is from $1,100 to $1,470. On a thirty-mile route the average is from $1,218 to $1,440. The difference shows up clearly, and is hardly fair to men covering the same distance under the same conditions. One is paid $100, $200 or $300 more per annum than the other.
I should like to cite just one or two instances. Take the sixteen-mile route. I think this will occur in many constituencies other than my own. The mail courier gets $1,000 for the sixteen-mile route, but at the same time the courier on a twenty-six mile route gets only $902.50. The man with the longer distance to travel is penalized to the tune of $97.50 because he has to deliver the mail ten miles farther than the other man. These things are unfair, and the couriers realize it. They expect the department to look into the matter at this time.
I want to cite one other instance, but the same discrepancies occur in a great number of cases. One mail courier with a seventeen-mile route to travel gets only $1,200. I know the route very well. He is not too highly paid at $1,200. But another man serving a twenty-eight mile route gets $1,100, $100 less because he has to travel thirteen miles farther every day. I ask the Postmaster General if this is fair. These things should be taken into consideration at this time; and, instead of tenders being called, the courier should have the right to renew if he has been satisfactory. Men of that type should have consideration. In fact, through all these mail contracts these discrepancies occur. I am not going to labour the point any further in favour of the mail courier.
Last year quite a number of hon. members spoke on this question, and with one accord they were all of the opinion that the mail couriers were the most faithful servants of any of the departments of government; yet they were the most poorly paid of all men, and no security was granted to them beyond the renewal of their contracts. These are things that I hope the Postmaster General will give consideration to at this session.

speechtext:
It is not my purpose to detain the committee for more than just a few moments. However I feel there are certain observations that I should offer. I agree with practically everything said by the hon. member for Queens. I doubt whether anyone who is familiar with the difficulties which have
Postal Service
been encountered by our mail couriers, difficulties which in the main they are still encountering, could do other than beseech the minister and his department to give immediate consideration to more adequate compensation for our mail couriers. I believe it was in 1941 that the government first recognized the necessity of making additional payments to certain mail couriers, largely because of the increased costs incurred owing to certain factors. Many of these contracts had been let prior to the outbreak of the war. Costs mounted rapidly during the first two years of the war, resulting in the five per cent bonus paid to certain couriers who ap-* plied, and under certain circumstances. I believe it was by order in council that that action was taken. Later on, further provision was made. I believe that three orders in council were passed, 2311, 5833 and 4960, authorizing additional payments to mail contractors who were operating under contracts which, from their point of view, were not equitable in view of changed conditions. My firm conviction is that the bonuses which have been paid are inadequate when one stops to consider for a moment the fact that the cost of living has increased by more than 50 per cent, or at least that the cost of living index has gone up to 151.
The resolution we have before us, if I interpret it correctly, authorizes the continuation of supplemental payments until March 31, 1949. I hope, even though it states that no such payment shall be made after that date, that nothing will stand in the way of the government taking whatever action may be considered appropriate prior to that time in order that supplemental payments be continued, or possibly I should say unless the government is prepared to take steps prior to that time to bring about a complete readjustment, quite apart from the bonus payments, in the method utilized in compensating mail carriers.
Speaking in the House of Commons on February 12, 1947, the Postmaster General made this observation with respect to tenders which were secured after tenders had been called for in connection with mail carriers:
It must be admitted that very often we have to refuse even the lowest tenders because they are too large. The tenderers do not know how their contract costs are going to run, where they will begin or where they will end, and they do not take any chances. Of course, when we succeed in obtaining a contract at what we consider a reasonable amount we grant it.
The information I desire in that connection is this. Upon what basis does the Post Office Department determine the reasonableness or otherwise of any given tender? I wonder if
they take into consideration the fact that over a given period the contract let, in, let us say, 1938 or 1939 was a certain amount but since that time the cost of living has gone up by a certain number of points. Have they taken that into consideration, or are they still thinking-

subtopic: MAIL CONTRACTS-SUPPLEMENTAL PAYMENTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: We have considered that and many other things.

subtopic: MAIL CONTRACTS-SUPPLEMENTAL PAYMENTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
-in terms of the 1938 or 1939 level? I am going to underline that question, hoping that the minister will not forget it, because this is what is occurring in certain parts of the west at least. The post office is calling for tenders and it is concluding in certain instances that the tenders are too high, or it takes the lowest of all, and says to the people of that area, "O.K. You have been enjoying mail delivery three times a week over that route, but since our costs are so high now we shall have to reduce your services to two days a week or one day a week".
I do not know whether the minister shook his head, but here is some correspondence relevant thereto with respect to one case in my own constituency where actually, in the interests of so-called economy, that is to say a few dollars, they have reduced the mail service to people in an old established community in that area. That case, as I am reminded by the hon. member for Bow River, was brought to the attention of the minister and the explanation was this: Well, sometime later-[DOT] the last correspondence is dated March 9- we will again call for tenders on this contract, and provided that someone will take it cheaply enough, we will restore the type of service which you enjoyed, let us say, ten years ago.
There is not a department of government that is able to show a more handsome profit on operations than the post office. In fact I believe the officials of that department speak with much pride of the profits which they obtain as a result of the operation of that service. In the light of that, it is extremely difficult for me to understand why, to use the common parlance of the west, they do so much chiseling when it comes to the mail delivery service or the postal service. It is something I cannot understand at all.
The district officers throughout Canada are endeavouring to provide the finest type of service which they can under the regulations, but they seem to be constantly haunted by the feeling that Ottawa has applied great pressure for economy.
I believe the Post Office Department and the minister himself have always prided themselves upon the type of service they offer. By and large they are quite justified in doing so,
Postal Service

but in many communities, just because an operation will not pay, as they say, it does not seem to matter at all whether the people have been living in the community for forty or fifty years, the department either refuse to give adequate service or deprive those people of certain existing services.
My argument, advanced on previous occasions and advanced here again tonight, is this. Certain operations cannot pay; but there is no reason, as long as the Post Office Department is piling up millions in the 'way of profits annually, why certain communities-and there cannot be many of them-should not be provided with at least a minimum service, even though that specific operation may not pay.

I rather thought my observations were right in line with the resolution before us. However, there is a possibility that I may have strayed a little afield and therefore I will not pursue that course further. I will ask the minister * the question I previously put. What basis is used to determine the reasonableness of a tender for mail delivery in any specific area served by a rural route?
If we could have something definite in that regard it would greatly help. We are in favour of the continuation of the payment of bonuses to mail carriers. We rather fancied that consideration might well have been given to increasing these bonuses because, after all, we must not forget that these men today are paying approximately twice as much for the automobile or truck they use as they paid ten years ago. Parts, gas and all their equipment have gone up tremendously in price during the last ten years; and no five per cent or ten per cent bonus will compensate them for this additional cost. Moreover, I can visualize

that the minister may encounter, if he has not already done so, considerable difficulty in securing bids in certain areas unless these rates are increased, with consequent reduction in the service that is rendered to certain of these communities. Possibly the minister might comment on my question,

speechtext: I know that the Postmaster General is just as much interested in this resolution as any of the rest of us. I should like to say that, after the full-dress debate we had a year ago, there is probably no necessity of having a repetition in 1948. speechtext: There is not much I want to say on this, Mr. Chairman, and I shall try to keep within the terms of the resolution. The supplemental payments were made because with the rise in prices and the rise in cost of living, the payments made under the contracts were not meeting the costs that many of the couriers were put to in fulfilling their contracts. The resolution provides that these supplemental payments shall be discontinued as of March, 1949; that is, in a little less than another year. I agree with the hon. member for Bruce who spoke a moment ago.

subtopic: MAIL CONTRACTS-SUPPLEMENTAL PAYMENTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes. The contract system in this matter has never worked satisfactorily. Couriers tendering for these routes tender for them, in many instances, at prices which could not pay them for the time and energy expended and the costs to which they were put.

Poor old private enterprise.

Mr. MaeINNIS: Yes, private enterprise; I agree with my hon. friend. While contracts in other businesses under private enterprise are quite proper and quite the thing to do, in these circumstances where the individual does not take into consideration all his costs and says that this is something he will take on the side, it does not work out satisfactorily and the service suffers.
What I was going to suggest to the minister is that, before the term of these supplements ends-and he has still some time before it does-he try to work out some policy for the payment of couriers that will eliminate the unsatisfactory nature of the tender system. Personally I do not think it can ever be made to work. Even now persons contracting tor routes cannot say wrhether the prices at which they contract will be satisfactory six months from now. speechtext:
I thank hon. members who have spoken. I want them to understand that I realize the difficulties of the department in granting these contracts. This government and the government before it took the attitude that the contractors were men and had the right to tender. They know what they are tendering for and they tender. I suppose they are all reasonable men. We have to take this into consideration. We cannot admit for one minute that these contractors are minors or children and that they must be protected. Otherwise where should we stop? Are we to stop at mail contracts, or must we do the same thing with regard to every employee and every thing that is being done in any of the departments?
I admit that there are so many factors to be taken into consideration that it is absolutely impossible to fix a rate, and I could give a great many examples. There might be ten, fifteen or twenty contracts in Canada that are alike. But the country is so large, the seasons vary so greatly and the ground is so different that if we were fixing a norm for contracts, we would have to fix one from one end of Canada to the other, which would be worse than the freight rates. It would be something which would require lawyers who were well qualified and who had made those rates a life-long study, in order to be explained properly.
This has been considered many times by the Post Office Department and by governments before the present one; and it was found that, after all, it was better to continue with the tender system. In 1941 or 1943, during the war, costs of gasoline, for example, were raised; and we gave a bonus to take care of that rise and the rise in various things such as oil, gas, and even automobiles. Later on we gave another bonus, by order in council, again in order to help them, because prices were going up. Labour was in short supply and it was difficult to keep on with these contracts.
After the war, all these orders in council had to cease after a certain time when peace was proclaimed legally by order in council. Then we passed this law last year because business conditions had not changed. They were sometimes even worse than during the war. We passed this law last year in order to help the contractors.
One hon. member was asking what were the norms that we were taking in order to grant contracts. In this, of course, we have to use discretion, because a man with a contract to carry mail on the north shore of the St. Lawrence must be paid more than a man who has a contract in the Niagara district, for example, where he can use an automobile all year.
There are many other things we may not know. A man may be of a certain age and have very little to do. He will tender at a price that suits him. He already has an automobile or a horse and buggy. He puts in a low tender. Sometimes he is doing something else as well. In most of these cases they carry merchandise or people when they deliver their mail. All this has to be taken into consideration ; and even if we were fixing rates, taking into consideration everything we could think of, I do not believe we would arrive at a better price than that quoted by the man who says, "I am prepared to take this contract at this figure". They do not make very many mistakes.
In this house we are sometimes liable to talk rather as a lawyer in court. We take one particular case and generalize on it, then draw conclusions; but I think we make a mistake in doing so. My department and I would like very much to be able to establish a rate in advance at so much a mile in this district and so much a mile in that district, but to do that one would have to take this part of the service and either put it under the civil service commission or fix the rates according to our discretion. Today anyone can submit a tender. It does not matter whether he is a Conserva-
Postal Service

tive, a C.C.F.'er or a Liberal; if he submits the lowest tender and has the machinery to enable him to fulfil his contract we give it to him. I know the difficulties that are created at times. Occasionally there are protests which I have to put aside, because we give the contract to the man with the necessary machinery to carry it out.

subtopic: MAIL CONTRACTS-SUPPLEMENTAL PAYMENTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: To get back to what the minister said a moment ago about a chap tendering and getting a contract, is there anything to prevent that man from obtaining a bonus after having obtained the contract?

speechtext: If the hon. gentleman reads the act we passed last year he will see the circumstances under which this gentleman may have a bonus. He must serve one year before he can ask for a bonus; and we must be satisfied that conditions have changed.

subtopic: MAIL CONTRACTS-SUPPLEMENTAL PAYMENTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Then do I understand that after the expiration of a year he is eligible for a bonus?

speechtext: He may ask for a bonus, and we will examine his case. He has to prove that he cannot fulfil the contract with a reasonable profit which will permit him to live; and under those conditions we grant him a bonus. I was explaining that if we were to get rid of the tender system the government in power would be able to take only its friends to fulfil these contracts. We know that could be done very easily, and we do not want that.

subtopic: MAIL CONTRACTS-SUPPLEMENTAL PAYMENTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I should like to ask another theoretical question. Let us say a certain man is given a contract because his was the lowest tender. After serving for a year, he applies for a bonus which, when granted, brings his salary above the figure of the next highest tender. What action would be taken in that case?

subtopic: MAIL CONTRACTS-SUPPLEMENTAL PAYMENTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: He carries on for one year and then proves that his contract figure is too low, that conditions have changed, or that he made a mistake. If his reasons are good, we give him a supplement. In a few moments I am going to give figures to show that we do not make very many mistakes.

subtopic: MAIL CONTRACTS-SUPPLEMENTAL PAYMENTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do not think my question has been answered. Let us say the next tender was less than the total of the first tender plus the bonus. What action would be taken in that case?

I said we would give that gentleman a supplement. The

man whose tender the year before was perhaps $50 higher has been eliminated; the other gentleman has taken the contract. He has served for one year, has bought his automobile or his horse, and we give him the supplement. I do not think we could do otherwise.
As I was about to say, if we did away with the tender system we would have a great many more employees who would be civil servants. I suppose they would have to be within the ages of twenty-one and sixty-five, and we would have to superannuate them after a certain number of years. We would like to do all that, but it must be remembered that in some cases contracts are given to men who are over sixty-five years of age. It is not a difficult job to go to the station, pick up the bags and carry them five or six or ten or fifteen miles and then go home. It may be just the sort of job an older man needs, and he knows what he should ask for carrying out that contract.

subtopic: MAIL CONTRACTS-SUPPLEMENTAL PAYMENTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: In referring to my question a moment ago, the minister said no one should know better than the tenderer what it is worth to carry mail over a specific route. Theoretically that may be all right, but in practice and in fact that is not the case. We have had instances in which five men have tendered, and the spread between their tenders has not been more than $100; yet the department has said all the tenders were too high. So I want to ask this question. When the officials go over a specific route and set a rate, or when they say a bid is too high, just how do they go about the matter? Do they set an arbitrary figure, or what factors do they take into consideration?

subtopic: MAIL CONTRACTS-SUPPLEMENTAL PAYMENTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The officials of the Post Office Department are men of wide knowledge. The man in charge of this department, for example, has had twenty or twenty-five years of service, and he knows. We have to protect the taxpayer as much as possible. We think of that sometimes in the post office. If tenders are much too high we certainly have the right to say so, and to ask for new tenders. This we do. Sometimes we arrive at a settlement with a man whose tender was too high, but who is ready to reduce it to a reasonable amount.
As hon. members know, all these laws are temporary. Perhaps .1 have spoken a little more than I should, due to all these questions which have been asked, but I might tell the committee that we have revenue postmasters, who are paid according to the amount taken in by their office. Today we are changing that and substituting civil servants who will be

Postal Service
paid a fixed rate. Many of them after serving for thirty-five or forty years withdrew from the service without any superannuation. We want to provide superannuation for these people. The department will then be able to sec that the place where a post office is installed in any village or town is a proper place.
We will pay for the premises instead of the postmaster paying as he does today under the revenue system. In addition the government will pay whatever employees are necessary to carry on the work. We do not want to continue in the haphazard way it was before.
We have thought of the mail contractors, but I must confess that we cannot find a better method than the one we have today. The cost of rural mail delivery is not going up any more. It went up between 1941 and 1947 but now it has reached the peak. I have some figures from April 1. 1947, to January 31, 1948-I have not the figures to March 31- so that lion, members can see what we have done.
A total of 2.297 contracts were granted with supplements, the total amount being $391,327. The contract rate before the supplement was granted last September was $1,704,248. The supplements that were granted prior to April 1, 1947, before the last supplements were granted by virtue of the law passed last year, were $279,300, so that the total cost, including all supplements, for those 2.297 contracts was $2,374,916.
The supplements granted between April 1, 1947, and January 31, 1948, increased the cost of service 19-73 per cent, while the supplements granted prior to April 1, 1947, by virtue of the orders in council of 1941 and 1943, increased the cost 16-39 per cent. The total increase in cost due to supplements was 39-38 per cent.
Certain contracts have had to be let by tender because the contractors did not want to carry on, because the contractor had died or for some other reason. When there is no contractor handling the mail we must call for tenders under the law. We called for tenders in 1,032 cases during the same period from April 1, 1947, to January 31, 1948. The former contracts, not including supplements, were for $671,495. The lowest tenders amounted to $924,550, so that there was an increase of $253,055, or 37-68 per cent, as compared with the other increase of 39-38 per cent where supplements were granted.
We want to abandon this sytem and go back to tenders. We had given notice to all mail contractors, but it was decided in council 5849-252J
that this should be extended for one year' more to meet the requests of hon. members from all sides of the house. I do not know what will be done in 1949, but we are asking for this extension at the request of hon. members.	*

subtopic: MAIL CONTRACTS-SUPPLEMENTAL PAYMENTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I want to assure the minister that we are not opposed to extending the bonuses, but I should like to know how the government handles certain of these cases. The minister pointed out a while ago the difficulties in carrying out certain routes, and I want to call to his attention the case mentioned a moment ago by the hon. member for Red Deer.
In this particular case apparently there was no question about tenders because only one man tendered. For reasons best known to themselves, the government decided that the. amount they would have to pay for this mail route was too high and that the only alternative was to cut the service. It seems tq me it is not logical for the minister to say that in some cases they must pay a bonus because the contract is too low and then in other cases cut the service because the contract is too high.
I happen to know this district exceptionally well. The sideroads are extremely bad, being heavy gumbo. That is probably why the minister never has more than the one tender. A service of three times a week has been given for a number of years. The man who had the contract renewed it. It may have been at a higher rate; I am not sure about that. The people in the district were much put out because the government, instead of giving this man a bonus to carry on the service, as was done in other cases, reduced the service. They paid the same rate but they reduced the service. I should like to know in how many instances the services have been cut instead of an increased amount being paid.

subtopic: MAIL CONTRACTS-SUPPLEMENTAL PAYMENTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I could not give the hon. member the exact number, although I would have that information when we are on my estimates. I admit that we make mistakes, but if we attempted to establish in advance a rate for all these routes the mistakes would be more numerous. In distant districts the mail must be carried in whatever way it is possible to deliver it. We deliver by dog sleigh, by plane, by courier' on horseback and in every way possible, for our motto is to deliver the mail everywhere, and not, as an hon. member said the other day, that the postman always knocks twice.
Sometimes the tender price is absolutely too high and we are not justified in awarding
Postal Service

a contract at that price. In one district in Quebec province which is represented by one of my closest friends here there is a route of twenty-five or twenty-six miles with quite a number -of boxes on the route, and the gentleman who had the contract was performing it for $770 a year. We called for tenders and that gentleman came in with a tender of $1,800 for the same service. I thought it would be practically stealing the taxpayers' money to grant the contract at $1,800, which was the lowest tender. So we called for new tenders, and this same gentleman put in another tender for $1,800. He was the only tenderer, so we had to cut the service because it was unreasonable to award a contract at that high price. We know, of course, the price at which. contracts in the surrounding district are being performed. It may be at $58, $60 or $65 per mile, and if we get a tender for $80 or $85 per mile in the same district, that seems too high and we have to protect the taxpayer. Sometimes we got the people on the route to agree to a service two or three times a week, instead of six days a week. We have to use our discretion.

Mr. MaoNICOL: Mr. Chairman, I know the minister is familiar with the matter I am going to bring to his attention and I bring it up to encourage him to take up with his departmental engineers the necessity of eliminating a vicious bottleneck in one of our internal transportation routes, the removal of which would be of great assistance and of material help to transportation between Montreal and New York City.
The Richelieu river route, leading from the great St. Lawrence river, was the first route to be opened up in the history of this country by the great Champlain, in 1609, and yet it is one of the most neglected transportation routes in our country. So far as I can understand it, there is no excuse for that whatever. I have been up and down the river nearly every year, because it is not only a very scenic route, but also a historic route. It was first opened to ship traffic about 1831, and on the whole there has been very little improvement in it since it was first opened up.
As one leaves Montreal and goes down the river to Sorel, a distance of forty-six miles, the draft is thirty-five feet. Of course, it would be out of the question to have a 35-foot draft from Sorel to New York city. After one leaves Sorel and goes up the river to St. Ours, a distance of fourteen miles, the draft is 12 feet. The minister's predecessor was a man for whom I had a very warm regard. I thought a great deal of him, and on several different occasions he brought up the question of improving the Richelieu river transportation to a draft of twelve feet from Sorel to Lake Champlain. I saw him shortly before he died. I told him that I would bring the matter up in the house until his hopes regarding the Richelieu would be fulfilled. If one leaves Sorel, as I said a moment ago, and sails up the river fourteen miles he comes to St. Ours where the draft immediately changes from twelve to six and a half feet. Notwithstanding the fact the river is a fine broad river from St. Ours, and a
Supply-Transport
fairly good draft in many places, the draft that regulates the course is six and a half feet.
The distance from St. Ours to Chambly is, I believe, thirty-two miles. At Chambly a very much worse bottleneck is met with. One then enters the old Richelieu river canal, and for a distance of twelve miles from Chambly to St. Johns the draft of the canal is still six and a half feet. That is the third change from Montreal. First is the 35-foot draft, Montreal to Sorel. The Richelieu river itself is twelve feet from Sorel to St. Ours; then from St. Ours to Chambly, six and a half feet, and then from Chambly to St. Johns, six and a half feet.
But the minister's predecessor did have in view having that river placed in proper condition. At St. Ours he built a lock. I remember supporting it. One of the first things I did when I came to the house was to support the building of a new lock at St. Ours. I believe the minister's predecessor built it standard size, 329 feet in length by 45 feet in width, with a draft of twelve feet. That beautiful lock stands there today with little traffic through it excepting small boats which go down or up the Richelieu canal from St. Johns to St. Ours.
In the canal from Chambly to St. Johns there are eight locks. They are all little ones, about 120 feet long and about twenty-three feet seven inches wide, with a draft of six and a half feet. The minister's predecessor had commenced to make quite an improvement in the river north and south of St. Johns. About five miles south of Chambly he built what is called Fryer's dam. I helped that through the house because I agreed with his argument that by building the Fryer's island dam we could have a 12-foot draft from Fryer's island right up to lake Champlain, and then it would need only five miles of canal to get down to Chambly.
I do not want to detain the committee for any length of time. I hope the minister will take this under advisement and do his best to carry out the program of his predecessor to have at least a 12-foot draft from Sorel up to Rouses Point, the international boundary, because from that point on, right on to the end of the Champlain canal at Whitehall, a distance of about 125 to 140 miles, there is a very good canal with a 12-foot draft. I have often gone down there to watch the traffic on that canal. It would do anyone good to go down to Burlington, Vermont, and on down to Whitehall, and down as far as Albany, to see the amount of traffic on this
Champlain canal. There is no reason why we could not have the same amount of traffic on the Canadian side. I hope the minister will direct his department to try to complete the canalization of the Richelieu river from Rouses Point to Sorel, which ls a fine city with a good elevator.
With the locks the same size as the St. Ours lock all the way up and down, I am quite satisfied that it would mean a great thing for the province of Quebec. It would mean more, traffic up and down the St. Lawrence river, particularly from the paper mills at Three Rivers, which would have an outlet right down to New York city. That should increase their export of paper to New York to perhaps a million tons a year. Today it is just a trickle. In addition to paper, the canal could be used for a thousand and one other commodities. It would be a real route from Montreal city to New York, a total distance of 452 miles, and all that distance would have a 12-foot draft at least. It would ensure a through, sound and safe 12-foot route from Montreal right down to New York city.
Once you get into the Hudson river, of course the draft is deeper. Not only that but they would have through the Erie canal, from where the Mohawk river and canal flow into the Hudson river near Albany, a 12-foot draft all the way to Buffalo. I am as sure as I am standing here it would mean a great thing to traffic in inland waters. Had it been there, it would have been of gigantic service during the war for the shipment of bauxite. It would have meant a safe inland route up the canal and all down to that beautiful town represented by an lion, member who is not in his-seat at the moment, Bagotville at the head? of Ha! Ha! bay, and they would use it today if the canal were there to be used. I cannot help saying to myself that it is not fair to that beautiful route which is a gorgeous scenic route; it is not fair to that part of the province of Quebec; it is not fair to all the territory of Quebec which would benefit from the deepening of that canal to 12 feet.
I do not want to go into the matter any further tonight because I am sure the minister wants to get some of his estimates through. I leave the matter with him and hope that he will take it up with his department. If he brings in next year an estimate to go on as far as Fryer's Island dam on the Richelieu river I shall support him. I should like to see him, as the successor to the man who introduced and promoted the real canalization of the Richelieu river, bring in a program for the completion of the Richelieu river canalization.
Supply-Transport

I feel I should say one word in reply to what the hon. member for Davenport has just said. I want to commend him on his advocacy of the Richelieu route which, as he says, was inaugurated, in so far as certain expenditures are concerned, by the former member for Richelieu-Vercheres, who was also one of my predecessors in the Department of Transport.
There is no doubt that that route should be given careful consideration. As the hon. gentleman has said, it is an historic route; it is also one that would be far shorter than the one which we use via the St. Lawrence at the moment, and great benefit could be derived from it. But I have to draw this to his attention-I think I did it when he brought up the matter during my estimates last year; if it was not last year it was the year previous to that-that when the international joint commission gave consideration to the Richelieu project-and they gave it very careful study- they came to the conclusion that it would not be advisable to deepen the route until such time as the St. Lawrence-great lakes waterways project had been completed.
There is a lengthy report on it to which I had to give some study when I was interviewed by a group of gentlemen representing the chamber of commerce from Sorel. As I recollect, the report was worded in such a way that, until such time as the greater project on the St. Lawrence waterway was completed, it would not be economic for the government to undertake the deepening of the route from Richelieu to the head of lake Champlain. However, I can assure the hon. gentleman that the matter is constantly before us, because representations are coming in from time to time. I am glad to see that he is taking such an interest in it.

I suggest to the minister that if he is wise he will not pay too much attention to the international joint commission in that particular. They did give consent when they allowed his predecessor to build the Fryer's island dam which would have meant a 12-foot route from Fryer's island to lake Champlain, with a little dredging near St. Johns. They gave consent, and it has not a solitary thing to do with the St. Lawrence seaway canal. It has no connection whatever with it. It is only a 12-foot route, whereas from the sea to Montreal it is a 35-foot route, and west of that it is to be twenty-seven feet. I do not think the St. Lawrence seaway has a single, solitary thing to do with the completion of the canalization of the Richelieu river. I hope the minister will give that full consideration and fight

against the argument that the canal cannot be completed. A 12-foot canal is one thing; a 27-foot canal is another thing, and a 35-foot route is something else. They would not put anything like that over on me. I read all the papers on the subject and I went to Burlington to listen to the discussions when the international joint commission sat. I cannot see how the two things ai'e connected. I am convinced of that, because they did allow the building of Fryer's dam. The Fryer's island dam was built but it is not in operation.
Was not the route practically abandoned when the export of hay ceased to be the principal item of commerce along the Richelieu?
I am informed that the route is used at the present time for certain products that are shipped through it.
There is a certain amount of live fish and some oil. Eels going into the market are taken alive in boats.
And paper products from Donnacona as well.

Has the minister the
revenue?
1 will have it in a moment.
There is no revenue because nothing much bigger than a rowboat can go up and down the canal today.

The amount of traffic that went down the canal in 1947 was 61,086
tons, and 538 vessels used the route.

There are one or two matters I should like to bring before the minister. I hope he will give some consideration, in the $60,000,000 estimates in his department, to the province of Ontario. One of the items in that $60,000,000 relates to the administration of the Transport Act. The administration of that act represents a large portion of the work of the transport department. I would point out that under the administration of the act the board of transport commissioners spend a large sum of money. The board, by the act, are required of their own volition to investigate complaints.
Is there any reason why the Toronto district should not have a steam suburban service? There is one in connection with the island of Montreal. It has been under the vote for almost thirty years. Montreal island has had an elaborate suburban service. On the other hand, it is in Ontario that the Canadian National Railways, through the old Grand
Supply-Transport
Trunk, made most of its money, and still we cannot get anything. I have had a great deal of correspondence with the board in this connection but we have not succeeded in getting anything. There is only one train a day that stops at Port Union. There is no reason why we should not have a service similar to that provided in the Montreal district. I am not complaining about the Montreal district, because it needs the service which it gets. That service has contributed to the solution of the housing problem in that magnificent city.
My complaint, however, is that the act is not being properly enforced. It is a dead letter for a similar service for the Toronto district. I do not wish to take up much time tonight because I know there are other speakers who are anxious to have the floor.
I must say, however, it is unfortunate that in an important department like this we have been given no opportunity so far this session to go into the work that is handled.
I should like to say a word now about the grade crossing fund. In our city we have spent several million dollars-$13,000,000 or $14,000,000-on grade separation through the Toronto viaduct straight along the waterfront. The city had no liability in that connection, because the railways came subsequently through the municipal highway, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company obtained a right of way all down the line from Leaside for $600 a year.
In connection with the harbour a great amount of money is also spent. The federal government has had two representatives on a board of five, and yet all the money that the government spends is spent through the Minister of Public Works. As I have pointed out before, we are the main taxpaying city in Canada, not only in the matter of income tax, customs and sales tax, but in other indirect taxes as well. In the Ontario cabinet we have five ministers representing our district, one being Premier Drew, and still we have had nothing but a goose egg since this government has been in power. We have had no representation from Toronto since 1935 in the federal cabinet.
My hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) came to our city the other day and we were indeed pleased to see him, but I must say that, while a large amount of money has been spent in his constituency and province, and in others as well, we have had nothing at all.
I must cover these points as quickly as I can, Mr. Chairman, and next I would point out that there are practically no lifesaving stations on the great lakes. Lifesaving stations
come under the marine section of the estimates, and while there may be a light here and a light there, there is really no protection, so that when some disaster overtakes us in the late fall from storms on the upper lakes the consequences are directly attributable to this lack of service. We have had three or four disasters on the great lakes, on lake Superior and lake Huron, but there are no lifesaving stations along that entire magnificent chain of great lakes. What have we to compare with the service provided on the United States side? Ten years ago there was a disaster on lake Superior and several sailors from Owen Sound and other lake towns died, and all they could do, before they perished, was to sound their sirens in the hope that some American ''fesaving station would come to their help. Several men belonging to Owen Sound, Col-lingwood and other ports were lost on these doomed ships.
There should be an investigation into the Hamilton accident at Burlington bay, and that investigation should start immediately, when a lift-lock bridge was raised for a ship and an automobile fell into the narrows there. Years ago there was a steamer known as the Corona. There was only about three and a half feet clearance for the boat on both sides of the ship in the old narrows there. The result was that the boat bumped into it and there were large sums of money spent afterwards there for retaining walls at Burlington beach at the entrance to Hamilton bay. It is a wonder to me that there was not a disaster there years ago.
There is no sum of money in the whole estimates here for lifesaving and all that kind of thing on the great lakes. There is no lifesaving station there, except the one at Toronto, which is paid for by the city taxpayers. When you consider the volume of traffic in the Welland canal today, in the Soo canal and the tonnage that is coming down from the lakes advancing the grain to the seaboard along the magnificent system of the great lakes, with no modern lifesaving stations, the department seems to be asleep. I am not blaming the present minister. Far from it, because we did not get a great deal of help from our own friends when they were sitting across on the other side of the house for a few years. In our city we depend on taxation on real estate to provide $65,000 a year for a lifesaving station. There should be such stations on lake Simcoe, Georgian bay, all over the Peterborough district as well as all the upper lakes and every place where a person has been drowned. The time has come when there
Supply-Transport

should be a regulated system of lifesaving on the great lakes through this department.
The minister represents an Ontario constituency. We seem to get nothing at all in Ontario because the Ontario members seem to me to be the same on all sides of the house. They are not like those from British Columbia, the prairies and the maritimes and the important industrial province of Quebec, who stand up here and assert their rights and privileges. I am not criticising any member for it, but I believe that we should have some fair treatment and should have equality of treatment. Since I have been a member of the house, I have never been one of those who objected to other people getting something. I believe in the principle of confederation, that what is for the good of one province is for the good of all; each for all and all for each. But with the tonnage of shipipng wre have on the great lakes, I think something should be done.
We hear talk about nationalism. When the storms were on in October, November and December, a few years ago, we had an example of the real kind of nationalism we have in this country. A Canadian ship, with Canadian sailors on it, sounds its siren hoping that a United States life saving station will hear it and save them from disaster. That is not fair to the shipping industry. It is not fair treatment to the men on the ship, many of whom are returned soldiers, to have a thing like this happen. I am pleading with the government to wake up and do something about the matter. We are not living in the last century; we are living in 1948. This coming fall, if the storms on the lakes are as severe as they were a few years ago, the ships on them are likely to suffer disaster.
Another thing I want to mention is this. My friend the hon. member for Queens, Prince Edward Island, obtained a 86,000,000 car ferry. I am glad to see him get it. He seems to be popular in the house. He has been asking and the minister has been answering questions on the orders of the day sometimes two or three times a week. I will not be surprised a bit if the hon. gentleman gets another $6,000,000 car ferry before this parliament closes. If he does get one, I will be glad of it.
Another thing I want to point out is that the old ship, the Northumberland, was brought up and put on the Port Dalhousie route thirty years ago. I would not travel on that ship to go to St. Catharines or Port Dalhousie. I was afraid it would go to the bottom of lake Ontario. Yet my friend the hon. member for Davenport went on it once. He had a Davenport picnic over there, but he did not take a 
chance by going on another picnic; otherwise he might have gone down to the bottom of the sea like McGinty. But I would say this. We need a car ferry in that district. A car ferry in that district has still greater possibilities because of the fact that a number of trains have been taken off by the Canadian National Railways. My former leader, Sir Adam Beck, said he wanted to electrify the whole Niagara district, and it would have been a blessing if that had been done. Electric trains would have been magnificent. We want a car ferry in that district running from Toronto to Port Dalhousie. One is badly needed at the present time.
There are just one or two other matters that I might mention. One is with regard to steamboat inspection. I would just call your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that one of the minister's predecessors told me we were to get a new boat on the Port Dalhousie route, but we have not got it yet and they are fitting out the old boat again for 1948. The hon. member for Davenport is coming in now, and I will call his attention to the chance he took of losing his life when he travelled in that ship on his picnic to Port Dalhousie. We ask for fair treatment..
With regard to the St. Lawrence, and power and navigation matters, may I say this. I think, in view of what has been said, some statement ought to be made by the minister either next week or the week after regarding power and navigation and regarding what is going on in the St. Lawrence. Today, under a vote here, we find that the minister has appointed another commission of investigation on the St. Lawrence in the Lachine section. We should have some statement from the minister before the house closes.
I do not want to take up too much time because the hour is now getting late. But I ask that we should have some consideration in the province of Ontario in these various expenditures. I think the railway commission should go out on its own volition and investigate these steam suburban matters.
There are many other things that might be referred to. One is the signal service and all that kind of thing, and the other provisions which have been made regarding icebreakers. One is badly needed in the province of Ontario, on lake Erie and lake Ontario, at the present time. When I visit the United States ports on lake Erie, or Buffalo, Geneva, Erie, Ashtabula, Cleveland, and all those coal places and see what we could have if we had ships, I am impressed. When I see some of the ships in dock on the United

States side of lake Erie, I think what a magnificent thing we would have if we had a fleet in lake Erie and right along in the lake ports in the province of Ontario, on lake Erie and navigation from Ontario to United States ports on lake Erie. I ask that some reasonable consideration be given to our province in these various votes, and especially to our city that gets nothing at all in these estimates. There are no votes for our city in the estimates of the Minister of Public Works or in the estimates of the Minister of Transport. I find no provision in the estimates for anything for our city, notwithstanding the taxes that they pay.
There is a vote in Ontario coming on now. We had reference made to it this afternoon. When the house opened today, reference was made by the leaders to our province and the other sister province. It seems to me that there is in the house at the present time too much politics and too little attention given to our own functions, privileges and powers with regard to the estimates. This is the eighty-fourth day of the session and we have spent only seven or eight hours of the whole eighty-four days on these various estimates of $2 billion. Yesterday the house was voting interim supply. By that you have taxation without representation. The House of Commons might as well close up if you are going to pass all these estimates in the antiquated way you have been doing so far. I ask for some reasonable allowance for our province from the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Public Works.

There is just one thing, Mr. Chairman, that I want to say in reply to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. It is that when he states that the province of Ontario gets nothing from the estimates of this department, he is entirely mistaken in that statement; and I am sorry he has seen fit to make it because it is wholly inaccurate. The province of Ontario gets a fair share. In some respects it gets far more than any other province does. I should like to take up briefly the matters he referred to, particularly with regard to the grade crossing fund. I should like to call the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact-
Mi-. CHURCH: There are no lifesaving stations there.

-that Ontario is far better treated than is any other province. I refer to the amount paid out of the grade crossing fund since it has been in existence. It amounts to $11,837,000. Out of that Ontario received $5,901,000, or 20-38 per cent. There
Sup-ply-Transport
was paid by the railways in respect to grade crossing projects, since the inception of this scheme, some $16,431,000. Ontario has received $13,704,000, so of the total Ontario has received 47-33 per cent. With respect of railwa}- services, the Canadian National spends far more money in the central region than in the other regions. That is necessary because of the traffic and because of the services which have to be maintained there. For 1948 the budget calls for an expenditure in the central region of $9,916,000 out of a total of $25,000,000. I could also give figures with reference to marine services, which I have not at my fingertips at the moment. So when the hon. gentleman says the province of Ontario does not receive a fair share of these estimates, he is wholly inaccurate.	.

On this general item I thought it might be appropriate to remind the minister that the people of our part of the country are beginning to feel their annual anxiety about the Hudson Bay route, as to which no doubt the minister expected to hear something from me. There seems to be a great deal of misunderstanding in regard to the increase in freight rates, if any, on the Hudson Bay road. I do not know -whether the minister will care to answer questions tonight; probably he will remind me that I should ask them and that he will answer them on the appropriate items. It has occurred to me that it may be some time before those items come up, and that I should make a few general remarks on my own account, whether or not the minister cares to answer them.
I shall be glad to answer them if I can.

First I would say many people do not have it well established in their minds as to whether the freight rates on goods other than grain have been changed at all on the Hudson Bay road. If the rates have been increased they are wondering upon what authority that was done, because apparently the Hudson Bay road is outside the system which applied for an increase in freight rates. If the rates on items other than grain have been increased in our part of the country we would be interested to know by how much and in what respects they have been so increased.
Again, there is a misunderstanding on the question of ocean rates from Churchill to British ports. About three weeks ago there was a report in the press congratulating the people in the Churchill vicinity on the fact that ocean rates had been equalized as between British ports on the one hand and Churchill and Montreal on the other. There was some
S upply- T tans port

rejoicing in the western press; as a matter of fact, one or two newspapers wrote self-congratulatory editorials on the matter. Certain correspondence was undertaken between the timber board of Saskatchewan and some British importers, however, and the board was informed that there was a difference of $11 per thousand in ocean rates on lumber as between Halifax and Churchill.
The minister is well aware that the Churchill trade lasts for only a certain number of weeks, I was going to say, or perhaps for only a certain number of days in the year. If we are to be ready for it preparations must be made in advance. Lumber is a commodity which has to be prepared, whether it is two-inch, three-inch or whatever it may be. Preparations must be made well in advance, and shipping space has to be arranged for such lumber. The port of Churchill was very successful in a small way last year. Unfortunately, because of the tremendous demand for grain, there was not, at the particular time it was necessary, enough grain in position to be shipped through Churchill, so I think only something like five million bushels were shipped through that port. We have always claimed that Churchill has never had a fair trial, and we believe it would be a good thing for the taxpayers of this country, as well as for the western farmers, if for once that port could be used to full capacity.
It did pretty well last year.
Yes, and if sixteen million bushels had been put through Churchill it *would have done a great deal better.
I agree.

I could make a speech on this matter, though I am not going to. We are anxious that we should have sympathetic understanding on the part of the minister and his officials, and that is what we are hoping to get.
You certainly had it last year.

There are other agencies at work which are anxious about this port, anxious in particular about reciprocal trade between western Canada and British ports. I am informed on good authority that the government of Saskatchewan-and surely in a matter of this kind, which is a national matter, we should not prejudice the issue if we mention the name of a government whose ideology is somewhat different from that of this government ; surely we do not have to face that sort of thing-is taking particular pains to talk

with various agencies in the old country about reciprocal trade between Britain and Saskatchewan. and they are anxious that some of that trade should be carried through the port of Churchill. I am told, for instance, that the government of Saskatchewan has on order now a good number of trucks and automobiles they want to bring to western Canada this year. Many other items could come through the port of Churchill, and we cannot see why they do not.
We realize, of course, that Churchill is better equipped for export, that is the export of grain, than for the import of goods. It lacks certain shed facilities and other things which I am not going into now. If this import trade does materialize and does increase I hope facilities will be provided at Churchill to handle that trade better than it has been handled in the past, as well as the purely export trade in grain. The other day someone told me that some repair work was going on at Churchill this year. I believe last year I suggested that certain repairs and additional work were necessary, and I am hoping some of it is now being undertaken.
The hour is late, and I do not know whether I can expect the minister, on a general item, to answer the questions I have raised. Incidentally, before coming to the chamber this evening I had not the faintest idea that this discussion would be coming up. I had prepared one or two questions to place on the order paper embodying at least some of the things I have asked this evening, particularly the question with respect to freight rates on the Hudson Bay road, and the rumour that ocean freight rates to Churchill had been lessened. I should be pleased, and I know it would set. at rest the minds of those in Saskatoon and Regina who are interested in this matter, if the minister could give some definite answer to the questions I have raised.

Mr. Chairman, coming as I do' from a section of Nova Scotia where the swift moving tides of the bay of Fundy merge with the mighty waters of the north Atlantic, where we are subject to fog, sleet and ice as well as all the normal dangers of navigation, I feel that I must say a few words regarding matters of marine. First of all, I wish to say I appreciate very much the co-operation I have always received from the minister.
Then, I want to suggest to the minister that an agency or sub-agency be established on the Nova Scotia side of the bay of Fundy. There is one operating in Saint John, but I think we need one on the Nova Scotia side to look after all the lighthouses and aids to navigation between Cape Sable and Point
Supply-Transport
Prim. A central area would probably be at Yarmouth, but I am not going to suggest what place. I think such a service is needed.
Then I consider we need additional icebreaking equipment. As the minister knows, we need additional buoy maintenance and lighthouse service ships. A large type of ship is needed, and I would suggest that these ships be constructed so strongly in the bows that they could be used for the dual purpose of ice-breaker and buoy and lighthouse tender. This is a very much needed service and probably the minister has it under consideration. I hope so.
I want to commend the minister for placing in his estimates an amount to cover the construction of a new lightship to take the place of lightship 14 which has been the guardian to the entrance to the bay of Fundy for over forty years. This is one of the few ships with an iron hull that is still in operation. I can assure the minister that this will be much appreciated by all of us who know the dangers of the Lurcher shoals. If the minister will take these few thoughts under consideration I am sure the people in my part of the country will greatly appreciate it.
I should like to say one further word with regard to a coastguard service. I do not suggest that any great capital expenditure be made over and above what is actually needed, but I suggest that we utilize all the available equipment we have in the air-sea rescue branch, the Department of Transport ships and the Department of Fisheries ships and then provide what additional equipment may be needed. We could have central offices or stations through which these services could be correlated so that relief could be sent at the shortest notice to any ship in distress. They would know just where to look for it.
As I say, I am not urging a tremendous increase in capital expenditure; I am simply asking that sufficient money be provided to maintain an adequate service at this time. Perhaps eventually this service will grow into something larger, but I think it is something that could be handled from a few offices to which the ships from the various departments could report and then be detailed to wherever rescue operations were needed.
I believe the minister was willing to answer my questions, but he did not have an opportunity to do so.
I am afraid I could not do so in the time that is left.

Perhaps we might call it eleven o'clock, because the subject matter I should like to take up would take
more than the two or three minutes that are available.
I should like to address some questions to the minister.
I would rather have the opportunity of answering the hon. member for Saskatoon City.
I was going to say something on the coastguard service which perhaps could be said in the two or three minutes left before eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for St. John-Albert wanted to ask some questions.
My questions will take only a minute.
That is what the hon. member for Saskatoon City said.
I have them written down, so I can make them brief.
I hope they are not on the Portland freight rates?

They are, but I do not expect the minister to answer them now. These are questions which I asked before the railway committee but did not get an answer. What were the operating expenses of the Canadian National Railway lines to Portland in 1947, and how much of that amount was paid in United States funds? Has there been an additional operating expenditure, or has there been an operational saving over the Canadian National lines to Portland since the reduction in freight rates became effective on November 17, 1947? I was told in the committee that I would be furnished with that information, but I have not received it.

I shall try to get answers to the questions for the hon. gentleman, but after listening to the second question I am afraid that it will not be possible to get that information. I should not like to say that I cannot get it until I have communicated with the officers of the Canadian National Railways.
I was told in the committee that the information could be furnished.
I would appreciate if the minister would make a comment on my questions.

I can do that if the committee will give me ten minutes, but I am not going to attempt to answer the hon. gentleman in one minute.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

Business oj the House BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On Monday we would like to move that the house go into committee of supply in order to call three new departments; probably public works, national defence and veterans affairs. After that., we shall continue with Bill No. 313, to amend the Supplemental Payments Act; next, the second reading of Bill No. 300, to amend the Canada Shipping Act, 1934. Then we *would move to revert to committee of supply to take up the estimates of transport, justice, post office and public works, although I do not know in what order we would proceed after transport.
Are we to go into supply first thing on Monday afternoon?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is the understanding that that will be the first order of business.
An lion. MEMBER: Public works?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It will be called, but it is the last on the list.
Will the housing bill. be up on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not on Monday.

With respect to the proposal to ask that three more departments be moved into supply on Monday, I wish to say that there will be no objection from this side of the house at any time to putting in as many departments as the government chooses; provided that each week the government will move to go into supply so that any grievances that hon. members may have can be spoken to. Our fear is that when you get so many departments into supply the time may come when you do not need to move to go into supply and we would be denied that privilege.
So far as we are concerned, put in as many departments as you like as early as you w'ant to in the session so long as you provide one opportunity in each week for hon. members to raise any questions that they may choose to raise.
There are only five or six departments in now'.

There would be one exception next week when the budget will be down. Since we shall be discussing the budget, it will not be necessary to ask for that, but I think this would be a reasonable arrangement and I urge the minister to accept it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe I can give that assurance, because there w'ill be six more departments to be brought in. When the budget debate is concluded, each week we shall make the formal motion to go into supply.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Are there not eight more departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not look over the list, but I am under the impression that there are six or seven more.
You may put so many departments in that some weeks no motion to go into supply may be made at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, yes, I will give the assurance that once a week, on one of the first three days of the week, we shall move to go into supply.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Monday, May 17, 1948
